name: Madness of the Machine God

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Madness of the Machine God

From each house to the next, it would seem whoever
lived there simply decided to leave, abandoning all
their worldly possessions. But one house in particular
is different: the door stands ajar, cupboards have been
swept bare of food save an overlooked moldy piece
of cheese or heel of bread. A safe that once guarded
precious or personal treasure sits open and the
wardrobe is vacant. Though the rest of the community is
oppressively silent and the evidence frustratingly scant,
this house has a secret to tell. Its master or mistress left
in a hurry.
A nearby village five or ten miles off might tell a
different story. Perhaps the fleeing homeowner reached
it, warned the residents, and was believed and taken
in. In such a place, one might have the opportunity to
meet with the eyewitness who fled. However, visitors
might encounter suspicious and wary villagers in
arms, who either refuse entrance or subject them
to inexplicable prodding and poking like the most
bellicose security guards.
But then, there is every chance the witness never made
it, or chose to flee into the wilderness, thinking it safer
sanctuary than another settlement. The next town might
be as quiet and bereft as the first, or it might tell a darker,
more brutal story.
In such a village, there is evidence of a fight. Homes
have been burned to the ground, dirt lanes and gardens
reduced to trampled mud. Things lie scattered about
like so much broken trash. Doors are ripped from lintels
and posts, furniture is smashed to kindling, and grisly

5

Wherever the Machine God goes, madness
follows. Spreading like a foul disease, the
Machine God’s influence bleeds into its environs,
about a quarter-mile at the end of each hour
it remains immobile, to a maximum radius of 5
miles. Whenever a creature within the area of
the Machine God’s influence completes a rest, it
must get a success on a Will challenge roll or gain
1d6 Insanity. Rather than becoming frightened
from gaining Insanity in this way, the creature
becomes fixated on its physical flaws or those it
perceives in others around them. If the creature
goes mad from gaining Insanity in this way, it
does not roll on the Madness table. Instead, it
becomes compelled and uses its action to make
“modifications” to the offending physical trait
using whatever means happen to be at hand—a
knife, a jagged piece of glass, a pair of rusty pliers.
The compelled affliction remains until the grisly
modification is complete, resulting in horrifying
mutilations, maiming, or death, unless the
compelled creature is restrained in some way or
rendered unconscious.
The Machine God typically remains in place for
2d3 days before it moves on, scrabbling away until
it vanishes altogether to reappear somewhere else
in the world.

name: Tracking the Horror

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Tracking the Horror
The caravan is difficult to follow, not only because
the tracks are muddled and incoherent, what with so
many hands and feet of varying description jerking
and pulling it along, but also because after a spree of
attacking and subduing a string of little towns, it seems
to disappear for weeks or months at a time. It sequesters
itself in dark, secluded forests and the shadows of
ominous mountain ranges to replenish its forces or
repair its fleshy mount. But eventually, persistent
characters might find what they’re looking for.

name: The Macabre Wagon

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
The Macabre Wagon
Once located, the caravan is much as it has been
described: a large, seemingly mundane covered wagon,
though it lacks horses to draw it or teamsters to drive it.

--- PDF p. 6 ---
Carrion birds wheel through the sky overhead, diving
from time to time to pick at the vehicle’s exterior before
rising once more, making their displeasure known
through caws and screeches.
A curious odor wafts from the wagon, growing
stronger the closer one gets: a reek redolent of
unwholesome meat still covered in hair, burning in some
infernal forge, fouling the air all around. When visitors
draw even nearer, they see what forms the covering
over the wagon’s bed—a multitude of faces patched
together with weeping crimson stitches, lashes in place
over empty eye sockets and mouths gaping. Where
bonnet meets bed, arms and shoulders once belonging
to children grasp perpetually at the empty air, with the
blind instinct to ensnare. The whole of it is supported by
dismembered arms and legs rather than wheels, fingers
and toes digging into the ground for purchase, straining
beneath a weight that would be too great to bear without
help from the multitude of evident victims who work in
concert to lift its unwieldy bulk.

name: Attacking the Wagon

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Attacking the Wagon

ATTACK OPTIONS

The Machine God defends itself from attacks by
transforming the wagon into a gigantic monstrosity.
Enormous appendages, each a horrid fusion of
machinery and flesh, lift the vehicle up, revealing
a frowning face, a grotesque mask fringed with the
reaching and clawing arms and hands that sprout from
its sides. In this form, the Machine God fights for a few
rounds before teleporting away.

name: The Flesh Forge

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
The Flesh Forge
Rather than attack the wagon, the player characters
might think to peer inside, looking through the flaps
at its back. If so, they see the interior of a space far
larger than what the wagon could possibly hold, room
enough for a dozen clockworks to stand at processing
stations in front of a roaring oven. Room enough for
them to rip limbs from bodies, eviscerate the remains,
and chuck discarded organs into the gaping maw of an
engine powered by flesh. Room enough for metalwork
to construct the gears that power bronze and copper
bodies once a soul has been ripped from the afterlife.
Room enough for cages holding hopeless, helpless living
mortals who await their turns for processing.
While nothing about this ambling monstrosity evokes
anything less than horrific despair, something else,
above all, resonates within its recesses. This is what
cows the captives within, robbing them of the ability to
scream or attempt escape: a pair of wide-set, monstrous
brown eyes above the organ-powered oven. They bulge
from the interior walls, bloodshot and wild as fire dances
across them. They blink slowly, but never fully close.
They watch all that happens and never sleep. When a
batch of viscera is tossed into the oven, they roll back
till the only color left is sickly white run through with
lightning bolts of red. Whether in pleasure or disgust is
impossible to discern.

makes its horrifying trait apply to all creatures that can

rolls made to resist its horrifying trait.

takes a fast turn and a slow turn each round. In addition,
it can use three triggered actions each round.

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Crushing Step)
Crushing Step A target creature falls prone and becomes
immobilized until the avatar moves or makes a stomp
attack. A creature immobilized in this way is blinded,
cannot stand up, and has total cover while it is trapped
under the avatar’s foot. At the end of each round the
creature is immobilized in this way, it takes 6d6 damage.
A creature immobilized in this way can use an action
to make a Strength attack roll with 2 banes against the
avatar’s Strength. On a success, the creature removes the
immobilized affliction from itself and crawls 1 yard out
from under the avatar’s foot.

SPECIAL ATTACKS
Double Attack The avatar makes two appendage attacks. It
can make a stomp attack in place of one of these attacks.
Moan of the Machine God The avatar’s mouth yawns wide
and emits a low, mournful moan that spreads out from a
point in its space into a 20-yard radius. Each creature in
the area that can hear the moan must get a success on a
Will challenge roll with 3 banes or gain 1d6 Insanity. Once
the avatar uses Moan of the Machine God, it must wait
1d3 rounds before it can use it again.

SPECIAL ACTIONS
Teleport The avatar teleports to a point in the world that it
chooses anywhere within 10d20 + 200 miles.

END OF THE ROUND
Epic Recovery The avatar removes one affliction from itself.
Spawn Horrid Clockwork 1d6 clockworks with the
horrifying trait spill out of the avatar’s body and stand
up in open spaces within its reach. These clockworks
can take the next available action. Once the avatar
uses Spawn Horrid Clockwork, it cannot do so again
until all the previous clockworks it has spawned are
incapacitated.

--- PDF p. 7 ---
A creature looking into the Flesh Forge from outside
must get a success on a Will challenge rolls with 3 banes
or gain 1d6 + 1 Insanity. While frightened from gaining
Insanity in this way, the creature is also compelled and
moves inside to patiently wait for the clockwork workers
to take notice and dismantle its body.
Any creature that climbs through the opening into the
room and sees the bulging eyes must get a success on a
Will challenge roll with 1 bane or gain 1 Insanity. While
frightened from gaining Insanity in this way, the creature
is also immobilized.

name: The Maddening Maze

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
The Maddening Maze
Two yawning alcoves flank the machinery at the far
side of the chamber and lead into a maze of passages
manifested by the Machine God’s horrid imaginings.
Each passageway leads to more corridors, stairways, and
chambers, some connecting to hidden rooms that hold
dreadful truths and terrible dangers. The arrangement
of these spaces changes with the thoughts of the
Machine God who waits somewhere within, making the
entirety of the labyrinth impossible to navigate.

7

name: Challenges

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Challenges

The maze has no fixed form. Characters might venture
down one corridor or climb up a staircase and then
turn back the way they came, only to find themselves
in an utterly unfamiliar environment. For this reason,
tracking the group’s progress uses an abstract method.
As characters explore the maze, they have opportunities
to gain revelations into the nature of the being. On
attaining the eighth revelation, they stumble into the
Heart of the Machine God, which is described below.
Opportunities for revelations result from rolls on the
following tables. Simply roll on the first table and then
consult the appropriate table for that encounter. After
the group successfully deals with the encounter, they
receive one revelation.
Revelations can take the forms of clues, such as
“Turn right at the next intersection”; clockwork keys
to open doors blocking the path; or lenses that, when
worn over the eyes, reveal glowing footprints on the
floor, hidden openings, or a ghostly hand that guides
the group for a time.

name: Oppressive Voices

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Oppressive Voices: As the characters explore the
maze, they hear murmuring voices emanating from the
walls, whispers that promise all manner of wild things:
incredible knowledge, astounding power, and the ability
to cheat death itself. After the group contends with a
maze encounter, roll 1d6 and multiply by 10 to determine
how many minutes pass before they come to something
else of interest. For every 30 minutes spent in the maze,
have each member make a Will challenge roll with 1
bane to avoid gaining 1 Insanity from the constant hum
of voices.

1

One randomly determined character in the group
must get a success on a Will challenge roll with
1 bane or become compelled for a number of
rounds equal to 1 + his or her Insanity total. While
compelled in this way, the character attacks to
maim another target character, believing that
person to be hiding something in his or her mouth.
If the challenge roll is a success or when the effect
ends, the targeted character spits out a revelation
that takes the form of a small key.

2

The group finds a puzzle box. It takes three successes
on Intellect challenge rolls with 2 banes to open and
reveal the revelation within. Each time a character
gets a failure on a roll, he or she gains 1 Insanity.

3

The passage ends at a high wall made of slowly
rotating gears and moving machinery. The only
way forward is by reaching a ledge 100 yards up.
Climbing the wall requires three successful Strength
challenge rolls with 2 banes. On a roll of 0 or less,
a character falls 11 or 22 yards, depending on the
number of successes gained so far. Each time a
character fails, he or she takes 1d6 damage from
the grinding of the wall. The characters find the
revelation atop the ledge.

4

A riddle has been etched onto the surface of the
wall. You can use an actual riddle you find on the
tubes of the internet if your players like solving
puzzles, or you can just have a player make an
Intellect challenge roll with 3 banes to learn the
revelation. On a failure, the character making the
attempt gains 1 Insanity.

5

The walls slam shut on the characters and contract.
Each character takes 4d6 damage, or half the
damage with a success on an Agility challenge roll
with 1 bane. A character can attempt to disarm the
trap by getting a success on an Intellect challenge
roll with 2 banes, which also uncovers the revelation.

6

Half the group (round down), with targets chosen at
random, must get successes on Will challenge rolls
with 2 banes or gain 1d3 Insanity. While frightened
from gaining Insanity in this way, the characters
perceive the other members of the group as being
mechanical monsters, dire enemies to be destroyed.
When no more characters are frightened from
gaining Insanity in this way, the character with
the most damage discovers a revelation hidden
somewhere on his or her body.

--- PDF p. 8 ---
Chambers

8

d6

Chambers

1

This room is filled with scrolls and books
containing all one might read about the state of
mortal souls and the construction of clockworks,
from the journals of Arnos the Tinker to a copy of
the Black Sun Manuscript. If the characters spend
30 minutes reading, they gain one revelation.

2

A crypt is filled with broken clockwork pieces,
some vaguely human, others decidedly less so.
Some have been relegated to so much debris,
some with worrying amounts of life remaining. All
are wicked or pained or mad. The first character
to sift through the mess must get a success on
an Agility challenge roll with 1 bane or suffer a
grievous cut, taking 2d6 damage. On a success
or a failure, the character finds a revelation. The
second character to do so (but no others) who
succeeds on the Agility challenge roll finds a
random enchanted object.

3

A chamber 30-yards wide and long has a door
at its far end. Tiles, each 1-yard square, cover the
floor. When a character steps on a tile, roll a d6.
On an odd number, the tile is false; it disappears
and the character must succeed on an Agility
challenge roll to avoid falling into darkness. A
character who falls reappears 1d20 yards above
the ground outside the wagon. The first character
to reach the door on the far side discovers
the doorknob can be removed and acts as a
revelation.

4

The characters reach a chamber filled with fire
that emits heat and light, but it is not real. A
character can attempt to “disbelieve” in the fire
by making an Intellect challenge roll with 3 banes.
That character can safely move through the room.
All others take 3d6 damage from the flames. At
the center of the room is a revelation.

5

The characters come upon a room filled with
mirrors. As they move through the place, their
reflections step free from the glass surfaces and
attack. The reflections count as animated corpses,
but any character who kills his or her reflection
must get a success on a Will challenge roll or gain
1 Insanity. When each character has killed his or
her reflection, the corpse of the last is revealed to
be carrying a revelation.

6

The characters enter a large, gloomy chamber in
the center of which floats a mechanical heart. If
the characters attack the heart, it unfolds into a
humanoid shape and fights back (as a golem).
Destroying it reveals a revelation.

source.reason: Explicit CUR-003 source reference; edition/permission not certified.

originalText:
Machine God: the young optimist turned madman,
turned Horologist, turned abomination, whose
children and followers have so perverted his original
vision that he is unrecognizable as anything other than
a roving monster.
The heart counts as an object with Defense 5 and
Health 100. Each time the characters deal damage to
the heart, it releases a psychic screech, forcing each
creature in the chamber to make a Will challenge roll
with 3 banes. On a failure, the character gains 1d6
Insanity. In addition, a promethean with Defense 20
and Health 200, whose body incorporates mechanical
upgrades, forms in the fleshy wall coverings, tears
free, and attacks the group. Each time the heart takes
damage after the first, the promethean either heals
1d20 damage or can immediately take an extra turn
beyond the normal restriction. If the characters destroy
the promethean, the heart takes 5d20 damage.
